title: Rights and Duties
description: Reading a life story and the documents that defend a right: the words of servitude and of law (a master, property, a slave, a field hand, a whipping, a penalty, hardship, burial, evidence, a trader, to hire, restless) and the difference between a biography and an autobiography; the passive voice, which the book works but never names - be in the tense of the active verb plus the past participle, in the present (is protected, are paid) and in the past (was adopted, were separated), in the negative and in the question; the three steps that turn an active sentence into a passive one (the object becomes the subject, the verb becomes be plus past participle, be keeps the tense); why the passive is chosen at all - when the doer is unknown, unimportant, obvious or hidden, in scientific writing, and in reports of accidents where the result matters more than the cause; the decision to keep by plus the agent when it carries new information or to drop it when it carries none; reading a passive sentence back - which noun is the subject that receives the action, who really does it, and when the sentence simply does not say; expressing displeasure at a situation and expressing intention; the language of equality (empowerment, oppression, commitment, promotion, gender, millennium) and the word families it is built on (oppress / oppression / oppressive, employ / employer / employee / employment); and the quantifiers of the printed grammar summary - a little with an uncountable noun, a few with a countable one, a lot of with both - with the meaning each of them carries
